title: Know your role
points: The prescriber orders the medicine. The pharmacist dispenses it. The RN decides what you may do for each participant and gives you written instructions.
Give medication only when the RN has authorized you in writing for that participant and task. The participant’s condition must be stable and predictable.
Report a change in condition, order or dose to the RN. The RN checks participant-specific competency at least annually.

title: Read the pharmacy label
points: Check the participant, medicine, strength, dose, route, schedule and special directions. Check allergies, expiration and the last recorded dose.
Match the label to the current order and the medication administration record (MAR). Stop and ask the RN about any difference.
The generic name identifies the drug. Its class describes what it does, such as relieving pain or lowering blood pressure. Color and shape alone cannot identify it.

title: Understand the directions
points: PO means by mouth. BID means twice a day. Follow the exact schedule on the order and MAR.
PRN means as needed. Follow the written reason, dose and timing. Ask the RN if a decision is unclear.
NPO means nothing by mouth. Check with the RN before giving an oral dose.
Write “daily” in full. The abbreviation QD can be misread.

title: Check the six rights
points: Right participant and right medication. Use the agency’s approved identifiers and match the label to the MAR.
Right dose and right route. Check how much to give, how to give it and the site if specified.
Right time and right documentation. Check when the last dose was given. Record this dose after the participant takes it.
Check the label against the MAR three times: when selecting it, when preparing the dose and at the final check before giving it.

title: Measure the dose
points: Use a marked medication cup or oral syringe. Household spoons vary in size.
Set the cup on a level surface and read the liquid at eye level. For an oral syringe, follow the device markings.
If the strength or units do not match the instructions, stop and contact the RN. Never calculate a new dose yourself.
Check with the RN before crushing, splitting or opening medication. If swallowing becomes unsafe, stop the oral dose and get help.

title: Use the ordered route and time
points: Follow the authorized route exactly. Oral, topical, suppository and approved premeasured inhaled medicines each require participant-specific instructions.
Follow the written time window. A 30-minute window applies only when specified. Contact the RN if a dose is late or may already have been given.
Rapid-acting insulin is time-sensitive. DSWs cannot give insulin injections, including sliding-scale insulin, under this Louisiana HCBS delegation rule.
Stay with the participant to confirm the dose was taken. Never leave a delegated dose at the bedside for later.

title: Recognize side effects and reactions
points: Know the expected effect. Report a new rash, vomiting, unusual drowsiness or other changes as directed.
Prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, supplements and foods can interact. Ask the RN before giving a new product.
For trouble breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, or unresponsiveness, call 911 immediately. Follow dispatcher instructions and notify the RN and office.

title: Clean your hands and equipment
points: Clean your hands before preparing medicine and after removing gloves. Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
For clinical handwashing, scrub all hand surfaces for at least 15 seconds. A full 20-second scrub meets this minimum. Rinse and dry.
When appropriate, rub hand sanitizer over all hand surfaces until dry.
Use gloves when contact with blood or body fluids is likely. Change gloves between dirty and clean tasks. Keep equipment and the preparation surface clean.

title: Store medicines safely
points: Keep each participant’s medicines in their own labeled packaging. Follow the label for temperature, light and refrigeration.
Store medication securely according to the plan. Keep it out of reach of children and pets.
Set aside expired, damaged, discontinued or unreadable supplies. Follow agency and pharmacy directions for refills, counts, returns and disposal.

title: Handle a refusal or error
points: A participant can refuse. Respect their decision, secure the medicine, notify the RN and document the refusal. Never force or hide a dose.
Report a wrong, missed, extra or uncertain dose promptly, even when the participant feels fine.
Tell the RN what was given, how much, when and what you observed. Follow directions and complete the required record. Call 911 for an emergency.

title: Take and report blood pressure
points: Have the participant sit quietly for five minutes, feet flat, back supported and legs uncrossed. Use the correct cuff on the bare arm supported at heart level.
Record both numbers. Systolic is the top number. Diastolic is the bottom number.
For adults, 118/76 is in the normal range and 135/88 is in the stage 1 range. Follow the participant’s written reporting instructions.

A top number above 180 or bottom number above 120 is very high. Without emergency symptoms, recheck after at least one minute and promptly report a confirmed high reading. With chest pain, weakness or trouble breathing, call 911.

title: Count pulse and respirations
points: With the participant at rest, use two fingers to feel the wrist pulse and count the beats. Count a full minute if the rhythm is irregular.
A usual adult resting pulse is 60–100 beats per minute. Recheck and report a resting pulse of 115 according to the participant’s plan.
One rise and fall of the chest is one breath. Count breaths per minute and watch for increased effort.
Record the reading, time and symptoms. Call 911 for severe breathing trouble.

title: Check temperature and changes in condition
points: Use the thermometer and site authorized by the RN. Oral means under the tongue. Axillary means in the armpit. Rectal measurement requires specific training, authorization and privacy.
Use the device as directed. Record its reading, unit, site and time. Do not add a degree to an underarm reading.
Report changes from the participant’s usual condition, including pain, dizziness or swallowing problems. Describe what you saw and what the participant said.

title: Document the dose and give handoff
points: The MAR is a legal record. After administration, enter the participant, date, medication, dose, route, actual time and your initials or signature.
For a refused or missed dose, record the reason using the agency’s procedure. For a PRN dose, document why it was given and the response at follow-up.
Record relevant vital signs, changes, who you notified and directions received. Chart promptly and use the approved correction process.
Protect privacy. At shift change, tell the next worker which doses were given, which are pending and who is following up.
